title: Fewer children, almost everywhere
standfirst: An interesting paper by Michael Geruso and Dean Spears on falling fertility rates around the world. According to their data, 67% of the world’s population now lives in a country where fertility is below replacement.

plates.name: The fall
plates.editorNote: Today, most of the world outside sub-Saharan Africa has fallen below that line.
plates.headline: The world went from 5.31 children per woman to 2.25 in sixty years
plates.body: In 1963 the average woman could expect 5.31 children; by 2023, 2.25, just above the 2.1 at which each generation replaces the last. 158 of 161 countries ended lower than they began. In the UN's projection for 2100, half the countries end between 1.58 and 1.89, and the world goes below 2.1 in 2050.
plates.caption: Total fertility rate: every country of a million people or more, and the world with the UN’s 80 and 95 per cent ranges.

plates.name: The crossing
plates.headline: Two in three people now live where fertility is below replacement
plates.body: Japan crossed 2.1 in 1957, the United States in 1972, China in 1991, India in 2020. Each circle is a country, sized by its people: 83 had crossed by 2023, home to 67 per cent of the world. The hollow ones cross in the UN's projection; 11 do not before 2100.
plates.caption: Each country of a million people or more at the first year its rate is below 2.1; area is its population in 2023. Above, the share of the world’s people in such countries.

plates.name: Twelve countries
plates.headline: Twelve countries, one scale
plates.body: Each panel is one country against the world in grey, on one scale. The UN projects 7 of these 12 to drift up from where they are now and the rest to keep falling; by 2100 all 12 are between 1.30 and 1.91.
plates.caption: Total fertility rate, estimated to 2023 and projected to 2100.

figure.scaleLine: Children per woman on one scale, 1950 to 2100; the world in grey; the value is 2023
figure.phoneScaleLine: Children per woman; the value is 2023

plates.name: The floor
plates.editorNote: There have been spikes, the Baby Boom being the famous one, but they were blips around a long-term decline.

quote.text: To put it bluntly, history offers no examples of societies recognizing very low birth rates as a social priority and then responding with effective changes that restore, and sustain, replacement-level fertility.
quote.credit: Michael Geruso and Dean Spears, “The Likelihood of Persistently Low Global Fertility”, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2026

plates.headline: Of 51 countries that fell below 1.5, none has come back
plates.body: 51 countries of a million people or more have gone below 1.5 children per woman. None has returned to replacement; the highest any has climbed back to is 1.89, in Moldova. South Korea, at 0.72 in 2023, is the lowest of them.
plates.caption: Total fertility rate of each country of a million people or more that fell below 1.5, from the year it first did. The scale starts at 0.5, not zero.

coda.label: At South Korea’s rate
coda.text: Arithmetic on one number, not a forecast: each generation is the last multiplied by 0.72 over 2.1.

zones.label: No country of a million people has come back up through here
zones.phone: None has come back up through here

plates.name: The peak
plates.headline: The world’s births peaked in 2012, in the UN’s central projection
plates.body: 146 million babies were born in 2012. Deaths rise as the world ages, and in 2084 they overtake births, the year the world’s population peaks at 10.3 billion. The range is wide: by 2100 the UN puts births between 85 million and 155 million a year.
plates.caption: Births and deaths in the world each year, with the UN’s 80 and 95 per cent ranges for births.

plates.name: Where babies are born
plates.headline: By 2100, almost one baby in two is born in Africa
plates.body: In 1950, 12 of every 100 babies were born in Africa and 62 in Asia. In 2023, 35 and 50. In the UN's projection for 2100, 48 and 38.
plates.caption: Share of the world’s births by region, estimated to 2023 and projected to 2100.

plates.name: India
plates.editorNote: And yes, India as a whole is now below replacement, though, like any country, with vast regional variation.
plates.headline: India went below replacement in 2020; its people keep growing until 2061
plates.body: India's fertility fell from 5.73 in 1950 to 1.98 in 2023, crossing 2.1 29 years after China. The population goes on rising because so many Indians are young: in the UN's central projection it peaks in 2061 at 1.70 billion.
plates.caption: India’s total fertility rate against the world’s, and its population, with the UN’s 80 and 95 per cent ranges.

plates.name: Why India keeps growing
plates.headline: Fewer babies, more parents
plates.body: In 2023 India had 115 million children under five and 128 million aged 15 to 19: the base of its pyramid has already narrowed. The bulge of young adults carries the population up for another 38 years. By 2061 the largest age group is 55 to 59.
plates.caption: India’s population by five-year age group and sex, 2023 and the UN projection for 2061.
